author: Grace Chen
title: Hurricane Katrina Lessons: 20 Years Later
text:
Twenty years after Hurricane Katrina, sociologist Alexis Merdjanoff shares crucial lessons for long-term disaster recovery and resilience.
Hurricane Katrina, which made landfall in Louisiana in August 2005, remains one of the most devastating natural disasters in U.S. history. It crippled Gulf Coast communities and displaced over 1.5 million people.
While the immediate mental health toll of disasters like hurricanes is well-documented—new analysis shows spikes in suicides and overdoses after the Maui wildfires and increased psychiatric medication use in California after wildfires—the long-term impact is often overlooked. What happens after federal aid dries up? Why do some bounce back while others struggle for years?
These are the core questions driving the research of Alexis Merdjanoff, director of the environmental public health program at NYU School of Global Public Health. As a sociologist, Merdjanoff investigates how populations recover and build resilience after major events, from Hurricanes Katrina, Sandy, and Ian to the Deepwater Horizon oil spill.
“Recovery programming often focuses on the first three to six months after a disaster, but people still need help after that time,” Merdjanoff explains. “They might not realize what they need until their housing is stable and their children are back in school. Then, they might need a small business loan or mental health services.”
For 15 years, Merdjanoff has been immersed in data from the Gulf Coast Child and Family Health Study. This longitudinal research, led by NYU School of Global Public Health’s David Abramson, follows over a thousand families in Louisiana and Mississippi who were impacted by Hurricane Katrina. Two decades later, she reflects on what this enduring study reveals about recovery.
The Lasting Echoes of Disaster
Strong social ties and community support are critical for resilience after disasters. Conversely, displacement can significantly harm employment prospects and mental well-being.
Merdjanoff’s research, using survey data from New Orleans residents, found that housing damage and being a renter were linked to greater emotional distress. These mental health challenges often lingered for over a decade. Notably, a delayed onset of PTSD symptoms was common following Katrina, a reality that short-term aid programs often failed to address.
While many Gulf Coast residents managed to return home, experiencing better mental health outcomes than those who relocated or faced unstable housing, others never returned. They established new lives elsewhere.
In a new study published in *Traumatology*, Merdjanoff identified three key factors influencing residents’ decisions to return to New Orleans or relocate: post-Katrina housing affordability and rising costs (including insurance and taxes); the strength of family ties and social support networks; and a deep-rooted attachment to the city itself.
Merdjanoff believes that the long-term impacts of Hurricane Katrina offer vital lessons. This research can help predict future mental health needs following other disasters, such as recent wildfires in California and floods in Texas.
She advocates for mental health services to be available for at least a year post-disaster, not just a few months. Targeted support for those displaced for extended periods is also crucial.
Federal recovery programs require long-term models and investment, but community-level efforts are equally vital. This includes empowering trusted local organizations. Embedding mental health services in schools, as was done in New Orleans after Katrina, or channeling housing assistance through existing community groups are effective strategies.
“A lot of the work has to be done at the community level, because so much of disaster recovery is about social cohesion,” Merdjanoff says.
Older Adults in the Face of Natural Disasters
While much disaster research has focused on families and children, Merdjanoff is increasingly examining the impact on older adults.
“People like to age in areas that are at risk for hurricanes, heat waves, flooding, and wildfires,” she notes, referencing the common desire to retire in warmer climates. “If you know older adults, they don’t want to leave their homes. So, what do they need to age in place in areas prone to climate-related disasters?”
To explore this, Merdjanoff has spent years talking with older adults in Louisiana, New Jersey, New York, and Florida, gathering their experiences following Hurricanes Katrina, Sandy, and Ian. Through interviews and surveys, she listens to their personal stories of disaster and recovery.
She’s found that older adults face heightened risks, not only due to health challenges or isolation. They are also prime targets for scams from predatory contractors, fake FEMA officials, or identity thieves seeking insurance or aid.
While some geographic differences exist—for instance, older adults in New York City report less loneliness, despite higher housing costs—common challenges and solutions have emerged across different locations. These findings have spurred Merdjanoff to develop a pilot program aimed at boosting disaster resilience among older adults.
This program, planned for testing in New York City, the Jersey shore, and Florida, will pair older adults with young people. Together, they will engage in preparedness exercises, memory sharing, and learning to identify and avoid scams. This collaboration fosters social cohesion and mutual learning. Older adults, often portrayed as victims, possess valuable experience that can enhance their own and others’ resilience.
“Older adults have lived through a lot. They may have lost a spouse or friends, or recovered from illness themselves,” Merdjanoff observes. “They’ve experienced enough to put things in perspective. How do we tap into this perspective for others and use older adults as a resource?”
Natural disasters may be inevitable, but their consequences are not. Merdjanoff hopes that a deeper understanding of their long-term effects across the lifespan will help communities avoid repeating past mistakes.
“It’s frustrating to see that the same things that happened in Hurricane Katrina also happened in Sandy and Ian and the recent floods in Texas,” she says. “We need to think creatively about how to apply the lessons from Katrina to prevent people from suffering the same consequences.”
